wine.name: L'Ermita
wine.classification: Gran Vinya Classificada of DOQ Priorat, the first so named, from the 2017 vintage
wine.grapes: Garnacha, the great majority, from old bush vines, with a little Cariñena and a few white vines planted among them.
wine.sites: L'Ermita, a steep slope of llicorella facing north east above Gratallops, below the hermitage of Our Lady of Consolation, with bush vines planted before the middle of the twentieth century.
wine.making: The bunches are destemmed by hand and the wine is macerated for about six weeks in oak vats, with the cap punched down. Malolactic fermentation and ageing follow in French oak, in the 2020s large oval foudres rather than new barrels, for a year to a year and a half before bottling.
wine.glass: Black cherry, raspberry and violet over dried thyme, liquorice and slate dust; deep, yet more floral and fresh than its weight suggests, with fine, firm tannin and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after five to ten and lasts two decades and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: Catalan for the hermitage: the vineyard takes its name from the chapel on the hill above it.
A great classified vineyard, the rung above Vinya Classificada on Priorat's own ladder; L'Ermita holds it from the 2017 vintage.
Priorat's appellation in Catalan, of the qualified rank that only Rioja shares in Spain.

records.table: L'Ermita is Álvaro Palacios's wine from one steep slope of old Garnacha on llicorella slate below a hermitage above Gratallops, the first Gran Vinya Classificada of Priorat. Deep yet floral and stony, it wants decanting and a large glass.
records.story: The founder was born into the family of Palacios Remondo, a wine house of Rioja, and studied oenology in Bordeaux, working at Pétrus as a student. In 1989, at the invitation of the founder of Clos Mogador, he joined the small group of newcomers at Gratallops who made their first wines together from that vintage, each sold as a clos; his label was Clos Dofí, the name that passed to the wine of Finca Dofí, his first vineyard. In 1993 he bought the slope that became L'Ermita: old bush Garnacha on llicorella facing north east, below the hermitage of Our Lady of Consolation, which gave the wine its name, and the first vintage followed that year. Around it he built a ladder of his own, from the regional Camins del Priorat and Les Terrasses through the Gratallops village wine to Finca Dofí and L'Ermita, and the family went on to make wine in Bierzo, at Descendientes de J. Palacios, beside Palacios Remondo in Rioja. Over the years the cellar moved from new barrels towards large oval foudres. In 2019 the denomination presented its ladder of village, site and classified vineyard wines, and L'Ermita was named its first Gran Vinya Classificada, from the 2017 vintage. For a sommelier it is the last rung of Priorat's ladder made plain: one slope, old Garnacha and slate.

Les Terrasses and Camins del Priorat are regional wines of the house, not second wines of L'Ermita.
Priorat is written DOQ in Catalan and DOCa in Castilian, a qualified rank it shares only with Rioja.

report: A search restricted to the house's own domain returned nothing, so the record stands on the DOQ's own pages for the classification and on two secondary sources for each other fact; Wine-Searcher's Q and A and Decanter's Spanish Icons were read through search and not listed for want of room.

The planting of L'Ermita is given as 1900 to 1940, as 1910 and 1940, and as the 1940s, so the record says the first half of the twentieth century; the plot's size differs between sources and is not given.

The élevage is twelve months in oval foudres in one recent account, about eighteen in others, and new barrels for the 2017, so the record says a year to a year and a half, in foudres in recent vintages.
Finca Dofí is dated to 1989 in one source and 1990 in another, so no year is given; Clos Dofí as its first name rests on one merchant and the library.

The technical sheets give between 85 and 92 per cent Garnacha, with a few white vines (named as Garnacha Blanca, Macabeo and Pedro Ximénez in one source only), hence the great majority and no names for the whites.

The Moueix under whom the founder worked at Pétrus differs between sources, and the one named in one of them is living, so neither is named; the founder himself is living and is described, not named, in prose.
Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35, one restricted to the house's domain (empty) and one shared with the group (the DOQ's ladder).

wine.name: Clos Mogador
wine.classification: Vi de Finca Qualificada, by the house's account the first wine in Spain so ranked
wine.grapes: Garnacha, about half, with Cariñena, nearly a third, and Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon for the rest.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyard around the cellar at Gratallops, which the house calls an immense amphitheatre of llicorella slate; the separate Manyetes parcel makes a wine of its own.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts in large oak vats or open 300 litre barrels, part of the fruit with its stems, after a long maceration of four weeks and more. The house's sheets for 2020 and 2021 give about eighteen months in 2,000 litre foudres; those for 2017 and 2019 a mix of 300 litre casks and foudres.
wine.glass: Dark cherry, blackberry and wild thyme over hot stone and graphite; full and warm, yet savoury rather than sweet, with firm, fine tannin and a long, dry, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed for five years or so, it opens slowly and keeps for twenty years in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: An enclosed vineyard: the word the newcomers of 1989 took from Burgundy for their estate wines.
A single estate rank, as the house describes it: grapes from the estate alone, bottled there.
The denomination, written DOQ in Catalan; Priorat and Rioja alone hold Spain's qualified rank.

records.table: Clos Mogador is the Gratallops estate that led Priorat's revival in 1989: Garnacha and Cariñena, with some Syrah and Cabernet, from its own amphitheatre of llicorella, fermented in oak and aged in large foudres. Warm, dark and savoury, it wants an hour in a decanter.
records.story: The house was founded by a winemaker of a family of French origin with a long history in the wine trade of Catalonia, who bought land at Gratallops with his family in 1979. In 1989 he drew a small group of newcomers to the village, and for the first three vintages, 1989 to 1991, the five pooled their grapes in one rented cellar and sold the wine under five labels: Clos Mogador, Clos Dofí, Clos Erasmus, Clos Martinet and Clos de l'Obac. The word clos, borrowed from Burgundy, named each as the wine of one estate. From 1992 each house made its own wine, and Clos Mogador kept to the family's vineyard on the llicorella around the cellar, and in time the house added Manyetes, from a parcel of Cariñena bottled apart, and a barrel aged white, Nelin. In time the estate gained the rank of Vi de Finca Qualificada, by its own account the first wine in Spain to hold it, a rank that asks for grapes from the estate alone. The cellar has since turned towards native yeasts, a share of stems in the vat and large foudres in place of small casks. For a sommelier Clos Mogador is the founding estate of the five clos: the house where modern Priorat began, savoury rather than sweet.

others.name: Manyetes
others.note: A wine of its own from the separate Manyetes parcel at Gratallops, led by Cariñena with Garnacha.

others.name: Nelin
others.note: The house's white, led by Garnacha Blanca and aged in barrel; a white, not a second wine of the red.

traps: The five clos of 1989 were Mogador, Dofí, Erasmus, Martinet and l'Obac; a later Priorat wine with clos on its label was not one of them.
Nelin is the white of Clos Mogador, not a second wine of the red.
Vi de Finca Qualificada is a single estate rank, not one of the village, site and vineyard rungs that the DOQ presented in 2019.

report: The founder, his wife and their son are living and are described, not named; the founder's name is already in people.json.

The origin of the name Mogador is given three ways (a novel about a family near Avignon, the old name of Essaouira, the vineyard itself) and is left out; so is the claim that the house took the name only in 1997, on one glossary alone.
The year of the Vi de Finca Qualificada is given as 2001 and 2006 in secondary accounts; the house says only that it was the first in Spain, so no year is given and the claim is told as the house's.
The founder's arrival in Priorat is given as 1977, 1978 and 1979; the record keeps the library's 1979 for the land at Gratallops, which the house's pages give too.

The family's French roots are placed at Gigondas in one source and at a domain called Le Martinet in another, and its Penedès firm rests on one glossary, so the story says only a family of French origin long in the Catalan wine trade.

The library's p-clos-mogador calls Nelin the reference for serious white Priorat, a judgement this tab refuses; the record says a barrel aged white. The plan writes Vi de Finca Qualificat; the house and the library write Qualificada.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, two restricted to the house's and the DOQ's domains, and one shared with the group (the five clos of 1989).

wine.name: Clos Erasmus
wine.grapes: Garnacha, the great majority, with Syrah for the rest; the share of Syrah moves with the year.
wine.sites: Seventeen terraces, old Garnacha among them, on a wooded hillside just outside Gratallops, on llicorella slate; younger vines and other parcels go to the second wine, Laurel.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented in oak vats after a maceration of about five weeks; the 2022 was fermented in concrete eggs and clay amphorae as well. The malolactic follows in barrel, then about a year and a half in French oak barrels, a share of them new, with a little of the wine kept in clay amphorae.
wine.glass: Black cherry, kirsch and incense over crushed slate and dried thyme; dense and dark, yet cut by fresh acidity, with fine, firm tannin and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and closed in youth, it needs eight to ten years to open and keeps for twenty and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle two hours ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Clos Erasmus is the tiny Gratallops estate of seventeen terraces, Garnacha with a little Syrah on llicorella, and one of the five clos of 1989. Dark and dense yet fresh, with incense and crushed slate, it needs years in the cellar and a decanter.
records.story: The founder, a Swiss newcomer to Priorat, bought seventeen terraces of vines on a wooded hillside outside Gratallops at the end of the 1980s and made her first wine with the 1989 vintage, among the five newcomers of the village. For three vintages, 1989 to 1991, the newcomers shared a rented cellar and one pooled wine, bottled under five names, and hers was Clos Erasmus. She named it for the humanist Erasmus of Rotterdam (about 1466 to 1536), an allusion to his In Praise of Folly and an answer to those who called the venture madness. From 1992 each house made its own wine, and hers stayed small: one hillside of terraces, Garnacha led, with Syrah beside it. The company took the name Clos i Terrasses, and the flagship kept the name of Erasmus. Laurel, the second wine, from younger vines and other parcels, takes its name from the meaning of the founder's Greek first name. By the 2010s a little of the wine was kept in clay amphorae beside the oak, and the 2022 was fermented partly in concrete eggs and amphorae. For a sommelier Clos Erasmus is the Priorat usually asked beside L'Ermita when an examiner wants the region's classic names: one hillside, old Garnacha and slate, made in small amounts.

wine.name: Clos Martinet
wine.grapes: Garnacha leads, with Syrah, Cariñena and small shares of Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, in proportions that move with the year.
wine.sites: Plots of the Mas d'en Martinet estate, within the municipality of Falset but in the Gratallops wine area, on llicorella slate with many different aspects.
wine.making: Long macerations, part of the fruit with its stems, of about five weeks; for the 2022 about half the wine, most of the Garnacha with a little Syrah, was made by carbonic maceration and blended back. The wine is then aged for more than a year in oak and other vessels before bottling.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and liquorice over rosemary and warm slate; full and ripe, yet fresh, with fine, firm tannin and a savoury, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of release, it keeps and gains for fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The house, named for its estate, the Mas d'en Martinet; a mas is a Catalan farmhouse with its land.
The flagship red, one of the five clos labels of Priorat's 1989 vintage.

records.table: Clos Martinet is Mas Martinet's red from the family estate in the Gratallops wine area, one of the five clos of 1989: a Garnacha led blend with Syrah and Cariñena on llicorella. Ripe yet fresh and stony, it wants an hour in a decanter.
records.story: The family behind Mas Martinet came to Priorat in 1981, by the house's account, and spent its first years studying the estate's slopes, rootstocks, grapes, climate and soil before it planted the vineyards that give its wines. The founder was one of the small group of newcomers at Gratallops who made the first clos wines together: for the vintages of 1989 to 1991 the group worked from pooled grapes in one rented cellar, and Clos Martinet was one of the five labels it bottled, beside Clos Mogador, Clos Dofí, Clos Erasmus and Clos de l'Obac. From 1992 each house made its own wine. Around 2000 the founder's daughter took charge of the cellar, and in that year, as the house tells it, it brought its vineyards, olive groves and woods together as one agroecological whole. Under her the house moved away from the methods of the revival's first years, towards long macerations with stems and a wider range of vessels than the small barrel, and for the 2022 about half the wine went through carbonic maceration. For a sommelier Clos Martinet shows the second generation of the revival at work on a wine of the first: the same estate and the same clos name, made with a different hand.

wine.name: Scala Dei Cartoixa
wine.grapes: Garnacha, the great majority, with Cariñena for the rest, from old vines.
wine.sites: Old vines on terraces and steep slopes of slate around Escaladei at the foot of the Montsant cliffs, between about 400 and 800 metres, with cooler clay on the higher ground.
wine.making: Each plot is fermented on its own in small cement vats, with about three weeks on the skins, and each vineyard is then aged apart for about eighteen months in 500 litre barrels and foudres before the final blend is made.
wine.glass: Red cherry, raspberry and dried thyme over fennel and wet slate; fresher and lighter on its feet than the Priorat of the lower villages, with bright acidity, fine tannin and a stony finish.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of the vintage, it keeps for ten to fifteen years in a good cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour or so; a large red wine glass.

label.means: Catalan for a charterhouse: the Carthusian monastery of Escaladei beside the cellar.
Latin for the ladder of God, the name of the monastery whose priory gave Priorat its name.

records.table: Cartoixa is the old vine red of Cellers de Scala Dei, the cellar beside the ruined charterhouse that named Priorat: Garnacha with a little Cariñena from high slopes under the Montsant. First bottled in 1974, it is fresh, red fruited and stony.
records.story: Carthusian monks founded the charterhouse of Santa Maria d'Escaladei at the foot of the Montsant cliffs in the twelfth century, at the wish of the Aragonese crown, the first house of their order in the Iberian Peninsula. The story goes that a shepherd had dreamt of angels climbing a stair to heaven on the spot, and the monks called it Scala Dei, the ladder of God. Its priors ruled the villages around, the Priorat, and planted vines. In 1835 the state's confiscation of church lands drove the monks out, and the buildings were left to ruin and fire. By the house's account, five families who had bought the monastery's lands founded a company in 1844 to make wine, the origin of Cellers de Scala Dei, and its bottles of Priorat de Scala-Dei won a gold medal at the Paris World's Fair of 1878. The cellar was refounded in 1974, and its first Cartoixa, of that vintage, is by several accounts the first wine bottled under the Priorat denomination. In 1991 the house ceded the ruined charterhouse to the Generalitat de Catalunya for its recovery, and in 2000 the Codorníu group of Penedès bought into the company. For a sommelier, Cartoixa ties the modern denomination to the monks who named it: Priorat bottled before the revival of 1989.

others.name: Scala Dei Prior
others.note: A younger red of the house, which by its account owes its mineral notes to the llicorella.

others.name: Masdeu
others.note: From the Masdeu vineyard, set above 650 metres on what the house calls a natural balcony over Priorat.

traps: Scala Dei is a place, a cellar and a monastery, not a grape or a style; the priory gave the whole region its name.
Cartoixa is the house's red, named for the charterhouse; the Cartoixa d'Escaladei itself is the monastery, ceded to the Generalitat in 1991.

report: The monastery's founding is given as 1194 by Wikipedia and 1163 by the Generalitat's heritage page, both at the wish of the same king (Alfonso II of Aragon, Alfons I of Catalonia), so the story says the twelfth century and names no king.

Founded is the house's own 1844, the company of five families it calls its origin; the house also says it was refounded in 1974, and other accounts date the families' purchase to 1840, so the integrator may prefer 1974.

The region record says the house has bottled since the 1970s; the house says its Priorat de Scala-Dei won a gold medal in Paris in 1878, so the story tells both and calls 1974 the first bottling under the denomination, on Spanish Wine Lover and The Drinks Business.
Codorníu's share of 2000 is 25 per cent in two accounts and a controlling stake in the Oxford Companion; the record says only that it bought into the company in 2000.
The departure of 1835 rests on Costa Daurada's tourist pages and Wikipedia; the fire that followed on Costa Daurada alone, so it is told without a date.

The house gives Cartoixa as 80 per cent Garnacha, a merchant 75; vine age (about 65 years) is volatile and left out. Its own sheets alone stand for the making and the Masdeu vineyard, as the house's own methods.
